titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State

div.head: 413. Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State
div.p: 4704. For Asst Secretary Abrams only from Ambassador Towell.
Subject: Advancing U.S. interests in Paraguay.
Refs: A. Asuncion 4653, B. State 317594, C. State 345774, D. State 344039, E. State 351103

2. With a three-day official mourning period decreed following the death of Colorado Vice-President Montanaro’s mother, which forced a postponement of my courtesy calls on senior Paraguayan officials, I take this occasion to slow the pace, step back, take a breath, and send you an abbreviated look at where we are since I arrived in Paraguay, and what comes next. My preliminary views on
Paraguay, and our perception here of what is to be done, are firmly grounded on my two extensive conversations with you before I left for post, your guidance to me following my initial meeting with Foreign Minister Acevedo (Ref B), the Secretary of State’s precise letter of instructions to me (Ref C) and, finally the detailed reporting cable of Under Secretary Armacost’s meeting with the new Paraguayan Foreign Minister, which confirmed that we are all speaking to the GOP with one voice (Ref D).

3. Relations with Stroessner: You gave me the challenging task of re-establishing a relationship/rapport with the President for the purpose of advancing U.S. interests, especially emphasizing the 3–D triad of democracy, drugs and derechos humanos. My first shot was the long-delayed, formal credentials ceremony where I advanced the less confrontational drug issue out front, rather than highlighting the more emotionally charged themes of democracy and human rights at what Paraguayans viewed as a ceremonial, not substantive, event. When I was then invited to sit on the gilded couch with Stroessner for a brief chat, the press hovered around us with lights and cameras for a significant portion of our time together, and I judged it imprudent to hold a serious bilateral exchange with the chief of state live on the evening news. As I left the palace, I told a senior GOP aide that I would like to have, at an unspecified future time, another, informal, substantive discussion with the President to go over a number of serious issues, when the President’s health so permitted. The morning of the next working day, another senior presidential aide contacted me and said the President would see me as soon as I wished. This same invitation was confirmed to me directly again this morning through a third senior GOP aide. Unless you think I should slow the pace, I plan to take up that invitation shortly and use that meeting to continue to carry out my instructions to build an effective working relationship with Stroessner so that I can attempt to advance U.S. policy interests directly with a man with whom we have had no bilateral link for some time.

4. I have just come out of a meeting with the new
Foreign Minister (septel) where my aim was-under the rubric of getting a readout on his Washington meetings with you and under Secretary Armacost—to drive home the point (lest anyone is still not getting the message) that U.S. policy, including 3–D, is constant; that you say it in Washington and I say it in Asuncion; and that the policy is bi-partisan and won’t change after the election, nor with the arrival of the new, smiling boy-Ambassador in Paraguay. I judge my meeting with Acevedo as a tentative success in my approach of seeking to advance U.S. interests in a careful, balanced and professional manner. And as I was unhinging my jaw to suggest to Acevedo what you in Washington proposed to him—that he get President Stroessner publicly to say in Paraguay what he said at the UN about GOP opposition to drug trafficking—at that moment, without coaching, Acevedo told me he has already recommended to Stroessner that he say publicly that very thing in Asuncion.

5. I want to assure you that I am firmly on board with the 3–D triad, which is the policy of the United States of America. At the same time, I firmly believe that a constant drum-beat recitation of all three elements—and with equal weight and equal volume at all times and in every forum—is not the most effective way to advance
our interests.

6. To put it bluntly, as Bob Gelbard did with Rose, our policy of public confrontation with the GOP failed. My country team feels strongly that three years of public friction with the GOP did very little to advance the three D’s. To be sure, we have won points with the Paraguayan opposition, and that is certainly helpful with the U.S. Congress and the human rights groups you and I talked about. I do not believe, however, that the approval of Paraguayan opposition is not the foremost goal of U.S. foreign policy here; advancement of the 3–D’s is.

7. I do believe, as does my country team, that to be effective on the three D’s we must build a closer relationship with the GOP and its top officials. We are not proposing a shift in policy. We are advocating tempering our public criticism and strengthening our private dialogue. I believe that public criticism is a more valuable policy tool when it is used sparingly.

8. The Secretary’s instruction to me urges “balance” in conducting our foreign policy here. That is exactly what I have in mind. In the short term it may give the appearance to some skeptical outsiders of a change in policy or a weakening of our commitment to the three D’s. In the long term, however, I believe it will bear fruit. If through quiet diplomacy we can persuade the GOP to move to direct elections of municipal officials in 1990, to enact electoral law reform so that the atomized non participating opposition will unite and participate, or to allow the Christian Democrats to hold their convention, I believe these would be real milestones on the long road to democracy. More importantly, our building a relationship with Stroessner and those around him would position us well to influence the transition towards post-Stroessner democracy in this country.

9. Interestingly, in the conversations Rose Likins has had with the opposition they have been the ones to advocate that we use more balance in our relationship with the GOP. The President of the Febrerista Party (Si Affiliate) told Rose that I should not visit the Casa del Pueblo—his party headquarters and scene of Clyde’s fall from grace with the GOP “because the USG has everything to lose and nothing to gain” from such an act, and that “You can’t get me out of jail if you don’t have a relationship with Stroessner.”

10. I am very much aware of the importance of maintaining our excellent relationship with the opposition. Even before I presented credentials, I used the pretext of Mike Shelton’s orientation visit here to meet with the wide variety of senior dissident Colorado and opposition figures well known in Washington, including Domingo Laino, Humberto Rubin, and Aldo Zuccolillo’s deputy at ABC Color. Realistically speaking, however, we recognize that real progress on at least two of the D’s may well not occur until Stroessner dies. Until then, we can try to chip away at the margins and prepare ourselves for the real work that will come in influencing the transition. Even then, changes are likely to come slowly.

11. In summary, I think we are on the right track here and, equally importantly, in tune with what you wish us to accomplish here. I have asked permission to come up to Washington to have Thanksgiving with my young daughter, and would like to meet with you and Mike Skol to review the situation and see if we need any major or minor course corrections.
12. As I am going to press with this, your 351103 is coming off the wire. If there are substantial points we have not covered above after we have digested it, I will be back in touch. Best regards.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880959–0507. Secret Noforn; Immediate; Exdis; Stadis.

In telegram 4653 from Asuncion, October 26, the Embassy wrote: “Following on the heels of Friday’s formal credentials ceremony with Stroessner at the presidential palace, the Ambassador began his first round of required courtesy calls on senior GOP officials early Monday October 24 with a visit to Chamber of Deputies President Luis Martinez Miltos. On October 25 he made back-to-back calls on long-time Colorado apologist and Senate President Gonzalez Alcina and departing Supreme Court President Argana. In each of these calls, the Ambassador reiterated the constancy of U.S. emphasis on democracy in its policy toward Paraguay and the bipartisan nature of this policy. He underscored the importance of combating narcotics trafficking and congratulated legislative leaders for imminent passage of a hard-hitting Paraguayan narcotics law.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880952–0148) In telegram 4603 from Asuncion, October 21, Towell confirmed that he had presented his credentials to Stroessner, the twelfth ambassador to do so. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880939–0029)

In telegram 317594 to Asuncion, September 28, the Department sent a message from Abrams to Towell, writing, in part: “As we discussed here it is important that your first steps be managed carefully to minimize the possibility that some might misinterpret a new style as a diminution in our support for democracy.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880868–0549)

Not found. In an October 21 letter of instruction to Towell, Shultz wrote, in part: “Relations with President Stroessner and his government are correct and should be so maintained as you and your country team seek to advance U.S. interests in Paraguay looking toward a post-Stroessner era. Recognizing the difference between the democratic system President Stroessner claims to have established in Paraguay and the basic elements of genuine democracies, U.S. interest are best served by 1) a peaceful evolutionary process that strengthens democratic forces and values within Paraguayan society, and 2) sustaining balanced, continuing attention to socio-economic development and human rights improvements. To achieve this evolutionary process will require your Mission’s contact with both the present government and non-governmental groups. Apparently, President Stroessner and mortality alone will determine his tenure in office. We do not expect the nature of his regime to change appreciably as long as he is in office, although, demographic, economic, and political pressures for change are evident.” (Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 31E, Paraguay)

Not found. In telegram 3805 from Asuncion, September 1, the Embassy recommended “that a bilateral meeting with Under Secretary Armacost be offered to Paraguayan FonMin Acevedo in conjunction with Acevedo’s travel to the UNGA. We believe it is important to use this opportunity, which coincides roughly with the arrival of a new U.S. Ambassador to Paraguay, to restate U.S. policy goals in Paraguay—narcotics, human rights, democratization—at the outset of Acevedo’s tenure as Foreign Minster.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880776–0803) In telegram 4687 from Asuncion, October 27, the Embassy reported on Towell’s meeting with Acevedo, writing: “Ambassador conducted a wide-ranging tour d’horizon with Foreign Minister Acevedo October 27 to discuss the latter’s visit to Washington and several matters of local business. In the course of the discussion the Ambassador reiterated the primacy of the three D’s—democracy, derechos humanos (human rights), and drugs—in U.S. policy toward Paraguay. The FonMin expressed his great satisfaction with his calls in the Department especially his meeting with Under Secretary Armacost. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880956–0193) No memorandum of conversation has been found.

In telegram 351103 to Asuncion, October 27, the Department sent a message from Abrams to Towell, writing, in part, that apparently “you concluded that it would not be appropriate to attempt to discuss with President Stroessner the importance the USG continues to ascribe to democracy and human rights. We certainly understand your concern about starting on the right foot with the GOP but we worry that Stroessner may be misled into thinking perceptions in Washington concerning his mode of governing have improved. As you know, they have not—and Foreign Minister Acevedo’s visit, at best, was an example of the GOP treading water and wasting opportunities.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880956–0031) In telegram 4378 from Asuncion, October 6, the Embassy reported on Acevedo’s travel plans including a visit to Washington “sometime between October 13 and 18 to call on OAS Secretary General Baena Soares.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880893–0552)
No memoranda of conversation have been found.

See footnote 5, above. In telegram 3309 from USUN, October 14, the Mission reported on Walters’ meeting that day with Acevedo, writing: “Ambassador Walters asked Acevedo if thought is being given to a likely successor to Stroessner. Ambassador Walters also encouraged Acevedo to make public GOP opposition to narcotics trafficking.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880917–0027) In telegram 342499 to Asuncion, October 20, the Department reported on Wrobleski’s October 17 meeting with Acevado “to discuss narcotics-related issues in Paraguay.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880931–0444)

In telegram 3269 from USUN, October 13, the Mission reported on Acevado’s statement at the 43rd UN General Assembly, including that he “reported that the Paraguayan legislature is presently occupied with the sanction of a new law to repress drug trafficking.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880912–00014)
No memoranda of conversation have been found.

In telegram 4757 from Asuncion, November 2, the Embassy wrote: “I was summoned to the palace October 31 for a twenty-minute one-on-one meeting with President Stroessner with no press in evidence. Although he may be a sick man, I also found him to be a rambling, nostalgic, frail old man living more in the past than in the present. I told him I wanted a frank, open and productive dialogue with him and his government, and thanked him for seeing me so soon after presenting credentials. I said that U.S. policy has not changed as a result of my arrival, explained our policy acronym 3-D (drugs, democracy, and derechos humanos) and discussed in depth why support for democracy was a basic U.S. foreign policy tenet. Going carefully so I would be invited back again, I was surprised that he took this all in seemingly pleasantly and didn’t bother to give me his standard civics lesson on Paraguayan-style democracy versus chaos. He spoke of Paraguayan friendship for and support of the U.S. (in D.R., at the U.N. etc.,) and rambled on amicably, keeping me when I made various moves to leave after an appropriate period of time. After my drug pitch, Stroessner reacted in a bizarre way: he spoke of the Chaco War (‘where I was wounded’) and expressed his concern that the U.S. is arming Paraguay’s former enemy Bolivia in the course of our war on narcotics. After twenty-minutes of conversation, he seemed to tire. He walked me to the door and invited me to return for further conversations. I will.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880974–0102)
